### Nama is name (not bending)
- In the suttas, nama used by itself means 'name'.
- The commentary (Paramatthajotika) explains it as 'bending' — immaterial
  states bend towards their objects. This is the standard Abhidhamma
  definition.
- "It may be that they thought it too simple an interpretation to
  explain nama with reference to 'name', particularly because it is a
  term that has to do with deep insight."
- "However as far as the teachings in the suttas are concerned, nama
  still has a great depth even when it is understood in the sense of
  'name'."

### The Sopaka story
- The ten questions Buddha put to the samanera Sopaka (attained
  Arahantship at age seven). "It is like asking a child: 'Can you count
  up to ten?'" All ten were deep, the tenth being on Arahantship. The
  second: "What is the 'two'?" — "Name and form."

### Name has conquered everything
- "Naman sabba anvabhavi, nama bhiyyo na vijjati, namassa ekadhammassa,
  sabbeva vasamanvagu."
- "Name has weighed down everything, nothing is more extensive than
  name. Name is the one thing that has all under its control."
- **Chinese parallel SA 1020** (CBETA, T02, no. 99): "名者映世間，名者
  世無上，唯有一名法，能制御世間。"

### The yoke of death
- "Akkheyyasannino satta, akkheyyasmit patitthita, akkheyyam aparinnaya,
  yogam ayanti maccuno."
- "Beings who perceive what can be expressed become established on what
  can be expressed. Not fully understanding what can be expressed, they
  come under the yoke of Death."
- "This shows that the word nama has a deep significance even when it
  is taken in the sense of 'name'."

### MN 9 definition (Sariputta)
- "Vedana, sanna, cetana, phasso, manasikaro — idam vuccatavuso, namam."
  (Feeling, perception, intention, contact, attention — this is name.)
- "Cattari ca mahabhutani, cat

### Name-and-form as reflection
"The discrimination between an 'internal' and an 'external' is the
outcome of the inability to penetrate name-and-form, to see through it.
There is an apparent duality: I, as one who sees, and name-and-form, as
the objects seen. Between them there is a dichotomy as internal and
external. It is on this very dichotomy that the six sense-bases are
'based'."

### The two views (Itivuttaka)
"Obsessed by two views, monks, are gods and men, some of whom lag behind,
while others overreach, only they do see that have eyes to see."
"It is as if one is trying to outstrip one's shadow by running towards
it out of fun, while the other is trying to flee from it out of fear."

### The sixty-two wrong views
"What it portrays is how the sixty-two wrong views lose their lustre in
the light of wisdom emanating from the non-manifestative consciousness
of the Buddha, which is lustrous on all sides."
"Those heretics who propounded those wrong views, conceived them by
dogmatically holding on to name-and-form."

### The tinted window panes
"Just as someone inside a closed room with tinted window panes sees only
what is reflected on those dark panes, and not beyond, even so, those
'seers' got enmeshed in name-and-form when they proceeded to speculate
on what they saw as their past lives."

---

### The perception of the compact (ghanasaññā)
"The worldlings under the sway of defilements, which thrive on the
perception of the compact, ghanasaññā, have the habit of grasping
everything... he regards the world as a unit due to his perception of
the compact, as he takes cognizance only of the arising aspect,
ignoring the decaying aspect."

### Delirium of views (diṭṭhipariḷāha)
"With reference to speculative views... the Buddha uses the term
diṭṭhipariḷāha, 'delirium of views'. Pariḷāha means 'delirious fever'.
Patients in delirium cry out for water. The worldlings, in general, are
in high delirium."
"Their views, based on wrong reflections, were mere hallucinations.
They kept on raising such questions, because they had no insight into
the nature of saṅkhāras, or 'preparations'."
"The worldlings spend their whole lifetime running in search of the
world's end. All that is papañca, conceptual proliferation."

### Wrong attention at the root
"The fallacy involved here, that is, the inability to understand that
their concept of the world is the outcome of wrong attention, we
illustrated by the simile of the magic kettle."

---

### The perception of permanence in the impermanent
"There is a malignantly pervert idea, ingrained in saṃsāric beings,
known as the perception of permanence in the impermanent, anicce
niccasaññā, which prevents them from seeing the inherent transience of
eye and forms. That is how the six spheres of sense create a world
before us."

### Sign-grasping and the influxes
"The tendency to grasp a sign in regard to the objects of the six
senses is the result of the perception of permanence. Due to the
perception of permanence, there is a grasping of signs, and due to that
grasping of signs, influxes flow in. Proliferations through craving,
conceits and views get heaped up. This is how our world is
constructed."
"Na nimittaggāhi nānuvyañjanaggāhī — 'he doesn't grasp a sign nor does
he dwell on its details'."

### Prolific reckonings (papañcasaññāsaṅkhā)
"One is carried away by prolific perceptions, papañcasaññā, and is
kept under the sway of worldly concepts and designations born of
prolific perceptions, papañcasaññāsaṅkhā."
"Proliferation creates things, giving rise to the antinomian conflict.
Duality masquerades behind it."
"The glue of craving and intoxicating influxes create a facade of a
real world before him. That is the world we touch with our hands and
see with our eyes."

---

### The Madhupindika three-act play
Act 1: Dandapani's question and the Buddha's enigmatic reply.
Act 2: The Buddha's explanation to the monks — even more enigmatic.
Act 3: Mahakaccana's exposition.

### The Buddha's reply to Dandapani
"According to whatever doctrine, friend, one does not quarrel with
anyone in the world... such is my doctrine, friend, thus do I proclaim
it."
"Dandapani shook his head, wagged his tongue, raised his eyebrows into
a three-lined frown on his forehead and departed, leaning on his stick."

### The seven underlying tendencies (the Buddha's summary)
"From whatever source papañcasaññāsankhā beset a man, if, in regard to
that, there is nothing to be delighted in, asserted, or clung to, then
this itself is the end of the underlying tendencies to attachment, to
aversion, to views, to doubts, to conceit, to attachment towards
existence, and to ignorance."

---

### The habit of taking signs
"It is because of our saṃsāric habit of taking in signs that thoughts
and proliferations arise in us."
"It is in the nature of some things that, though they have to be given
up, they cannot be fully dispensed with." (Hence the middle/gradual
path.)

### Delight as the world-fetter
"To delight enfettered is the world, thought is its trailing along."

---

### The mula-pariyaya (24 concepts, 4 persons)
"Earth, water, fire, air, beings, gods, Pajapati, Brahma... the seen,
the heard, the sensed, the cognised, unity, diversity, all, Nibbana."
The four persons: untaught ordinary person, monk in higher training,
arahant, Tathagata.

### The worldling's view (mula-pariyaya)
"He perceives earth as 'earth'. Having perceived earth as 'earth', he
imagines 'earth' as such, he imagines 'on the earth', he imagines 'from
the earth', he imagines 'earth is mine', he delights in earth. Why? I
say that it is because he has not fully comprehended it."

### The sekha's view
"He understands through higher knowledge earth as 'earth'. Let him not
imagine 'earth' as such... Why? It is because it should be well
comprehended by him."

### Maññati (methinks)
"Here it refers to an indulgence in a deluded mode of thinking under
the influence of craving, conceit and views."
"The word maññati, methinks. One usually methinks when a simile or a
metaphor occurs, as a figure of speech. But here it is something more
than that."

---

### The house and tiles relativity
"One might think that a house is made up of tiles and bricks, but tiles
and bricks themselves come to be because of a house. There is a mutual
relationship between them."
"If one raises the question: 'What is a tile?', the answer will be: 'It
is an item used for building the roof of a house'."
"There is no need to get down to an atomistic analysis like nuclear
physicists. Wisdom is something that enables one to see this relativity
penetratively."

### The child's hut
"Little children sometimes build a little hut, out of fun, with a few
sticks and shady leaves. When the mother creeps into the improvised hut,
she does not seriously entertain the concept of 'a house' in it."
"To the Emancipated Ones, the sandcastles of adults appear no better
than the playthings of little children."

### The arahant uses convention
"That monk might still say 'I speak', he might also say 'they speak to
me', being skilful, knowing the world's parlance, he uses such terms
merely as a convention."

---

### The duality held in fetters and grasping
"These fetters are called saṃyojanāni. A binding or a fetter implies
'two', as when two bulls are tied together. The term upādāna... implies
a holding on to something. There, too, the notion of a duality comes
in — one who holds and the thing held."

### Identification with attainments
(The infinity-of-space example, quoted in full in Section 2: a subtle
me-thinking attaches even to formless attainments.)

---

### The tides of imaginings
"Steadied whereon the tides of imaginings no longer occur in him."
"The idea behind this occurrence of tides of imaginings is quite often
represented by the concept of asava, influx."

### Consciousness dwelling
"The form element, householder, is the abode of consciousness. The terms
oka, niketa and nivesana are synonymous, meaning 'abode', 'home', or
'dwelling place'."
"The nature of consciousness in general is to abide or dwell in. That
nonmanifestative consciousness, however, has got rid of the tendency to
abide or dwell in."

### The three kinds of feeling
"The sage observes these three kinds of feelings, pleasant, unpleasant
and neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant, as they arise and cease dependent
on specific contacts, thereby gradually bringing the mind to equanimity."
"He understands it to be impermanent, uninvolved, unrejoiced."

### The two views (Itivuttaka, continued)
"Gods and men delight in existence, they are attached to existence...
When Dhamma is being preached to them for the cessation of existence,
their minds do not reach out towards it."
"Being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted of existence as such, some
delight in non-existence."

### The mirror creates the self
"Whether one has a liking or a dislike for what one sees, one gets the
notion 'this is me'."

### The grammatical framework
"There is a certain deep significance in the word yathabhuta. In
contradistinction to the two words bhava and vibhava, the word bhuta
has some peculiarity of its own."
